body.text: Democrats in the United States won control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives in the November 3 midterm elections. U.S. President Donald Trump said on election night that he would accept the results. The outcome deepens the lame-duck status of the president, who is barred from seeking a third term. The question for Seoul and Washington is whether the new balance of power in the U.S. Congress will change the alliance and U.S. policy toward North Korea.

On November 5, South Korea’s senior presidential spokesperson Kang Yu-jung said the alliance had developed over more than 70 years with bipartisan support from the United States. She added that no single election result would affect the alliance. The statement points to alliance stability that does not depend on which party controls Washington.

Indeed, the alliance has rarely enjoyed matching governments. For most of the past two decades, the presidents of the two countries have belonged to opposite political camps. Each mismatch has prompted the same complaint: that clashing ideologies leave the allies unable to coordinate on North Korea smoothly. That overstates the difficulty.

Presidents of both parties have pursued the same goal of ending the North Korean nuclear program. Republican U.S. President George W. Bush (in office 2001-2009) negotiated with Pyongyang in the multinational Six-Party Talks. His Democratic successor Barack Obama (2009-2017) waited for Pyongyang to change course under a policy called “strategic patience.” Their methods differed, but the destination did not. Each administration ultimately held that sanctions relief and other rewards should come in return for nuclear steps by Pyongyang and not in advance.

There was one U.S. president who changed Washington’s conventional approach on North Korea: Donald Trump. During his first term, Trump met North Korean leader Kim Jong Un three times between 2018 and 2019, pursuing a leader-level deal with Pyongyang. At the time, progressive Moon Jae-in was South Korean president. Progressives in Seoul had long wanted this kind of direct U.S. engagement and found common ground with Trump – who is decidedly not a progressive – on North Korea policy.

There were other sources of friction in the alliance, however, mostly related to money. Trump kept pressing Seoul to pay more for about 28,500 U.S. troops stationed in South Korea. Trump’s use of tariffs against both allies and rivals alike added to the pressure.

Both Trump’s North Korea policy and his tariffs were undone by the Biden administration – and then put back into force once Trump regained office. Beyond the specific policies, the back-and-forth reflects a fundamental truth that has long plagued the alliance’s approach to North Korea: Leaders in authoritarian states stay in power while leaders in democracies change.

Even if Trump were to meet with Kim and reach some sort of deal, Pyongyang has reason to question whether any agreement will survive the next election in Seoul or Washington. The U.S. Congress can write commitments into law, but the protection is limited – and it’s unlikely whether the incoming Democratic Congress will support any deal Trump might make with North Korea anyway.

What can keep policies consistent across administrations is a clear, shared view of Pyongyang. North Korea began laying mines and building fences along the line dividing the two Koreas in 2024, after Kim defined relations with the South as those between two hostile states. North Korea no longer has any interest in unification, or even dialogue, with the South. Pyongyang will not give up nuclear weapons because they now define the state. Closer ties with China and Russia, both of which have dropped all references to denuclearization, give North Korea more leverage to hold its course.

In response to that reality, Seoul and Washington should drop the hope that friendly dialogue can change Pyongyang’s course. Washington has no reason to lift sanctions in advance or to withdraw troops from the Korean Peninsula when Pyongyang is moving in the opposite direction. North Korean state media reported on October 30 that Kim urged scientists to accelerate the development of military artificial intelligence and unmanned aircraft. More unmanned weapons and more weapons of mass destruction are likely to follow.

Seoul has to answer the North’s buildup with greater strength of its own, because the peninsula sits on the front line of a new Cold War. At their October 2025 summit, South Korean President Lee Jae-myung and Trump agreed to pursue nuclear-powered submarines for South Korea. Wartime operational control of its own forces should return to Seoul. Security ties with the European Union and with partners such as Australia and India should grow at the same time. The goal is a South Korea able to defend itself without outside help.

Neither capital should chase talks that Pyongyang has not requested. Trump is signaling willingness to meet Kim again while Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of the North Korean leader, demands an end to “hostile” U.S. policies first.

If Pyongyang does come to the table, the allies should treat the meeting as a negotiation and not as the start of a relationship. Preparation at home must precede any such meeting. Strong military and intelligence capabilities would ensure that a failed deal costs South Korea nothing in security. The midterm elections changed the balance of power in Washington, but the task for Seoul remains the same.
